column3: Names defeat at that locus, the closest direct echo of the focus outcome.
Shows that a heavenly army is not needed for decisive action against a people.
Presents a fully gathered hostile host, clarifying the collective-force dimension.
Shows factions diverging and facing a grave consequence.
The preceding challenge to control of mercy frames the defeated faction's pretension.
Makes armies an exemplary subject whose apparent force is bounded.
Shows confederate threat producing avoidance rather than dependable fighting.
The immediate sequel identifies earlier peoples as the same kind of factions.
Contrasts visible factions with unseen forces that aid believers and punish deniers.
Adds another case of factions splitting and facing punishment.
A single cry extinguishes a collective, sharpening the focus's routed-host image.
Contrasts the defeated parties with Allah's party, described as successful.

The prior challenge to ascend through means exposes the faction's lack of sovereignty.
Directly states that an assembled force will be defeated and turn its backs.
Shares the scene marker but concerns believers tested under siege.
Completes the passage's catalogue: collective rejection of messengers brings punishment.
Names divine forces alongside inward tranquility, but only broadly relates to the host.

Earlier generations cry out when no escape remains, anticipating the focus's rout.
Locates the armies of heaven and earth under Allah's authority.

Affirms victory for Allah's party, but remains a generic party contrast.

An elite follows a ruler's unsound command, explaining how a people cohere wrongly.
A smaller faithful force can overcome a larger army by Allah's permission.

Invokes the day of factions as a historical warning to a people.

Loss at the decisive moment is a terminal but non-collective parallel.

The rhetorical question about Sijjin has no focused connection.

States a historical defeat, supporting the contingency of visible dominance.
The striking calamity is a remote consequence parallel only.
Return to the Fire supplies a generic end without factional structure.

The name of the striking calamity is only a remote consequence echo.

Facing an opposing army, believers seek steadfastness and divine aid.
Breaking bonds and spreading corruption gives only an indirect pattern of collective loss.
Unseen forces lower the deniers' word, a broad counterpart to defeated opposition.
The provision dispute and humiliation do not clarify the focus's host.
Divergent responses to a parable offer only a distant division parallel.
Provision and self-wronging do not add to collective defeat.

The reciprocity statement does not clarify the focus.

Promised angelic reinforcement directly contrasts human host size with divine aid.
Further angelic reinforcement sharpens the insufficiency of an opposing massed force.
Locates victory in divine reassurance rather than in the number of either side.
Forbids collapse after conflict and frames eventual superiority by faithfulness.
Terror is cast into the deniers' hearts, an interior mechanism of a host's defeat.
Makes help and abandonment decisive for prevailing, not collective resources alone.
Sets believers and deniers in opposed allegiances, with the latter's strategy called weak.
Answers an appeal for aid with a thousand angels in succession.
Defines angelic reinforcement as reassurance and firmness rather than autonomous force.
Divine intervention fixes believers and destabilizes those who deny in battle.
Prohibits turning backs when the opposing force is encountered.
Defines retreat from battle as a grave failure except for tactical movement or joining a force.
Relocates decisive action in battle to Allah while preserving human participation.
Declares that the sought decision has arrived and warns the opposing side to desist.
Commands steadfast remembrance when a force is met in battle.
Links internal dispute to failure and loss of collective strength.

States that the sent servants are the ones given help.

The immediate continuation contrasts their arrogance and schism with repeated prior destruction.
The faction's demand to hasten its allotted punishment extends the same passage's defiance.

Restrained hands in a conflict show divine control over the course of collective violence.

Apparent opponents lack durable unity and will not fight together except from protection.
The image of a compact battle rank clarifies the organized host form presupposed by the focus.
Pharaoh and Thamud recall exemplary collective powers placed under judgment.
The elephant-host's destruction is a direct paradigm of an army's defeated design.
Its strategic plan is rendered lost, clarifying defeat as collapse of collective purpose.
An unexpected dispatched force overturns the invading host.
The hostile army is struck by a means outside its own military capacity.
